transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-11
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Sophie Lee (Quantum Retail - Head of ML), Carlos Mendez (Platform Engineer), Priya Nair (VP Product)

Summary: quick discovery to understand Quantum Retail's reliability requirements, incident tolerance expectations, and to map hosted vs dedicated vs private trade-offs. Customer cares about multi-region failover, fallback policies to smaller/cheaper models, SLOs for latency and availability, and compliance (KMS/audit). Next steps agreed: send security pack + SOC2, run capacity calc, schedule deeper technical follow-up.

Topics:
- Current pain: single-region incidents, slow failover
- Fallback strategies: model variants, degraded-mode responses
- Multi-region routing and DNS/anycast options
- SLA expectations and reporting
- Observability and audit logs for incidents
- Pilot scope and timeline

Action items recap (from call): see action_items metadata above.

Transcript (timestamps approximate):
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone thanks for hopping on, um, really quick intros - I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, and with me is Ethan our SE.
[00:15] Sophie (Quantum): Hi, Sophie - thanks. We've got Carlos and Priya on as well. Our main ask today is around reliability concerns as we scale - especially incident tolerance.
[00:28] Ethan (Redwood SE): Great - can you walk us through a recent incident so we can understand impact and desired behavior?
[00:34] Sophie: Sure. Last month we had a region go flaky, our in-house serving backed off and, uh, we saw a 35% increase in p99 latency and some 5xx rates. Failover was manual - we didn't have automated routing and the app degraded hard. Customers noticed.
[01:02] Carlos: To add, we peeked at cache priming after failover and cold KV cache added like 300-400ms per request for a subset of calls. That was brutal on checkout flows.
[01:18] Ethan: OK that aligns with what many folks hit. With Redwood we can do a couple of things - multi-region routing with automatic failover, prefix/KV cache warming strategies, and fallback to smaller model variants to keep latency tight while capacity is rebalanced.
[01:40] Priya: When you say fallback to smaller models, does that mean we lose quality or is there a graceful degradation?
[01:47] Ethan: Good question. The typical pattern is a tiered policy: primary model (high-quality), then a compatible distilled or quantized variant that preserves semantic behavior for most prompts. You can configure thresholds - error rate or latency triggers - that cause automatic switching. We also support canary policies and staged rollbacks.
[02:10] Sophie: How fast is the failover? In our case we have a 3s budget for checkout-related prompts; p95 must stay under 1s ideally.
[02:20] Maya: For hosted, our multi-region routing plus warm standby can failover within tens of seconds to a couple minutes depending on cache hit-rate - if you want sub-second tail latency even during failover we recommend a combination: pre-warmed replicas in second region + fallback model with reduced compute (quantized) to keep token latencies low.
[02:45] Carlos: So we'd be paying for warm standby? How does that impact cost?
[02:50] Ethan: There's a cost tradeoff. Warm standby (reserved capacity) adds baseline cost but you get much faster recovery. We can model it: either you accept a slightly higher cost with dedicated reserved capacity per region, or you rely on cold capacity and have fallback policies to smaller models plus queuing. We'll send a spreadsheet to model your traffic pattern.
[03:14] Sophie: Are there built-in SLAs for multi-region? We need contractual guarantees.
[03:20] Maya: Our hosted API has published SLAs for availability on committed plans; Dedicated can come with stronger SLA terms and custom SLOs as part of an enterprise contract. For Private deployments you manage SLAs but we offer consulting to validate setup.
[03:36] Priya: We also need audit logs and end-to-end tracing for incident postmortems. Is that standard?
[03:43] Ethan: Yes, Redwood Console provides request-level traces, token-level latency breakdowns, and audit logs. For Private deployments we support forwarding logs to your SIEM; for Hosted we offer log export and longer retention as an add-on.
[03:58] Carlos: Encryption/KMS - we need BYOK and HSM support for keys. That was a blocker in previous evals.
[04:05] Maya: We support KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS) and HSM options for Private. We'll attach the KMS/HSM section in the security pack.
[04:18] Sophie: From a routing perspective, how do you handle DNS TTL and DR? Do you use anycast, or do you rely on regional endpoints?
[04:27] Ethan: It depends. We offer regional endpoints for isolation and anycast-based fronting for low-latency global routing. For strict failover control customers often prefer regional endpoints with our smart-routing layer that does health checks and fails over at the edge. DNS TTLs are configurable; we can also do traffic steering based on latency/health.
[04:50] Priya: What about partial degradation vs full failover - can we degrade non-critical features first?
[04:56] Ethan: Yes, Redwood supports route-level policies. You can mark routes critical (checkout) and set them to use reserved pools or pre-warmed instances. Less critical routes can be routed to cheaper models or queued. We also have built-in rate limiting and priority queuing.
[05:15] Carlos: Any real-world numbers? Example failover times, p95/p99 deltas when switching to smaller model?
[05:22] Ethan: In our internal benchmarks we've seen fallback to a 4-bit quantized variant reduce per-token latency by ~30-50% depending on hardware, while quality drop is minimal on many prompt types. Failover with warm standby can be <30s; cold start to on-demand GPUs depends on cloud provider and can be a few minutes. We'll share a benchmark sheet and a sample runbook.
[05:45] Sophie: How do you ensure model state and KV cache consistency across regions?
[05:51] Ethan: Good point - KV cache is per-replica; we provide strategies: replicate hot prefixes, prioritize prefix caching for critical flows, or accept a warm-up window. For stateful sessions we recommend sticky routing or shared external state store depending on latency tolerance.
[06:12] Sophie: Does Redwood do synthetic traffic to warm caches preemptively during incidents?
[06:16] Maya: We can run scheduled warmers and work with your team to prime critical prefixes. For Dedicated/Private customers we can automate cross-region priming during maintenance windows.
[06:32] Priya: On contractual SLAs - what downtime exemptions exist (force majeure, maintenance)?
[06:37] Maya: Standard exclusions apply. For enterprise Dedicated we can negotiate maintenance windows and notification SLAs. We'll share the SLA doc.
[06:49] Carlos: Observability: we need token-level cost breakdown per route, and per-customer attribution for our tenants.
[06:58] Ethan: Redwood Console already surfaces token-level cost and latency per route and per API key; for multi-tenant setups we have fine-grained tagging and export hooks.
[07:12] Sophie: If we do a pilot, what's a recommended scope to validate incident tolerance?
[07:17] Ethan: Pilot typically includes: 1) Traffic mirror of a subset of production requests to Redwood in two regions; 2) Configure fallback policies for critical routes; 3) Simulate region outage and measure failover times and user-facing latency; 4) Run quality regression checks. That gives you quantitative data in 2-3 weeks.
[07:40] Priya: And for dedicated reserved capacity, do we get isolation guarantees?
[07:45] Maya: Yes, Dedicated gives GPU pools reserved to your account with predictable throughput. You can configure autoscaling and burst policies. For strict isolation and compliance, Private deployment is the option.
[07:58] Carlos: Any examples of customers who ran incident tests and how it went?
[08:03] Ethan: We had a retail customer that did an automated failover test - by using warm standby and prefix priming they reduced user-visible errors by 90% and cut p99 increase in half versus cold failover.
[08:16] Sophie: Regarding data residency - we have EU customers and want logs and audits in EU only, is that doable?
[08:23] Maya: Absolutely - we support region-specific retention and can deploy Private control plane or Hosted regionally with EU-only retention. We'll include that in the security pack.
[08:36] Carlos: A couple technical clarifications: 1) when fallback to quantized model happens, do you keep request semantics identical? 2) How is rollout orchestrated?
[08:45] Ethan: 1) We ensure API contract and prompt handling stay the same; responses may be slightly different but we run automated evals to detect regressions. 2) Rollouts use canaries and A/Bs with automatic rollback on error thresholds; configs are versioned.
[09:02] Sophie: For our checkout path, what would you recommend as a conservative policy?
[09:06] Ethan: Reserve a small cold spare pool in second region, enable fallback to quantized model for p95/p99 thresholds, and set priority queuing so checkout requests bypass heavy batching delays. Pre-prime hot prefixes during traffic peaks.
[09:24] Maya: Also important - define SLOs and an incident playbook: who runs hotfix, paging, and which fallback triggers are manual vs automatic.
[09:33] Priya: Can you share an example incident playbook?
[09:36] Ethan: Yes - we'll attach a sample playbook and runbook in the follow-up.
[09:42] Sophie: One more question - how do you handle cross-region consistency for model updates? If we push a model change in one region, is there a window where versions differ?
[09:52] Ethan: We version models and support coordinated rollouts; you can pin model versions per region or allow our rollout engine to stage updates with canaries. There is always a short window on rolling updates but our rollout tools minimize divergence.
[10:06] Maya: Time check - we have ~32 minutes left, happy to go deeper on any of these areas or shift to pricing.
[10:14] Priya: Let's clarify next steps and pilot scope - we want a technical deep dive with infra next week (prefer Mon/Tue) and the security pack ASAP.
[10:25] Maya: Noted. Ethan - you'll do the capacity calc and attach benchmark sheet?
[10:29] Ethan: Yep, I'll run numbers and share a blank template you can fill with traffic shape.
[10:34] Carlos: We'll extract representative traffic for the pilot and share sample sizes.
[10:38] Sophie: Also please include guidance on the expected cost delta for warm standby across two regions vs fallback-only approach.
[10:45] Maya: We'll provide a cost model.
[10:48] Priya: Any legal/contractual red flags we should be aware of before the pilot?
[10:53] Maya: For a pilot we usually do a short-term MSA addendum; major clauses (data residency, KMS, incident reporting) we'll surface in the security pack.
[11:06] Ethan: Quick note on tooling - we can instrument synthetic traffic to warm caches and run chaos tests to validate failover. We do that for pilots if you want.
[11:18] Sophie: That would be valuable. Ok - thanks.
[11:22] Maya: Great. Quick recap of next steps: Maya sends security pack and SOC2 docs; Ethan runs capacity calc and shares benchmark template; Customer to share traffic shape; schedule technical deep dive on 2025-03-18 (TBD exact time).
[11:42] Priya: Sounds good. We'll aim to get traffic shape and a couple times for the 18th.
[11:48] Maya: Thanks everyone; we'll follow up in email with links.
[11:53] Carlos: Thanks.
[11:55] (call ends)
